claim: Id1-Venus reporter cells were generated using a targeting construct designed to express a fusion between Id1 and Venus from the endogenous Id1 locus.
source: We generated Id1-Venus (Id1V) reporter cells using a targeting construct designed to express a fusion between Id1 and Venus from the endogenous Id1 locus (Nam and Benezra, 2009) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation method and cites Nam and Benezra, 2009 as the source of the targeting construct design.

claim: The Id1-Venus targeting strategy has previously been demonstrated to faithfully report Id1 expression.
source: This strategy has previously been demonstrated to faithfully report Id1 expression (Nam and Benezra, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nam and Benezra, 2009.

claim: Id1V is readily detectable at E6.5 throughout the proximal epiblast with expression declining more distally.
source: Id1V is readily detectable at E6.5 throughout the proximal epiblast with expression declining more distally (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The highest levels of Id1V mark regions of the epiblast fated for mesoderm and surface ectoderm but not neural fates.
source: The highest levels of Id1V therefore mark regions of the epiblast fated for mesoderm and surface ectoderm but not neural fates (Cajal et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cajal et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2013.

claim: The majority (>65%) of Id1V+ cells in the proximal epiblast co-express Nanog.
source: The majority (>65%) of Id1V+ cells in the proximal epiblast co-express Nanog, with this proportion increasing to >80% within the posterior regions of the proximal epiblast (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The proportion of Id1V+ cells that co-express Nanog increases to >80% within the posterior regions of the proximal epiblast.
source: The majority (>65%) of Id1V+ cells in the proximal epiblast co-express Nanog, with this proportion increasing to >80% within the posterior regions of the proximal epiblast (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The majority (>80%) of Id1V+ cells do not express T.
source: In contrast, the majority (>80%) of Id1V+ cells do not express T, indicating that they are neither specified nor committed to a mesodermal fate at this stage of development (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Id1V+ cells that do not express T are neither specified nor committed to a mesodermal fate at E6.5.
source: In contrast, the majority (>80%) of Id1V+ cells do not express T, indicating that they are neither specified nor committed to a mesodermal fate at this stage of development (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Most (>80%) of the T+ cells at E6.5 co-express Nanog.
source: We also confirmed that most (>80%) of the T+ cells at this stage co-express Nanog (Figure 1H,I), confirming that T marks not only differentiating mesoderm but also pluripotent epiblast cells with a proximal posterior positional identity (Osorno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: T marks not only differentiating mesoderm but also pluripotent epiblast cells with a proximal posterior positional identity.
source: We also confirmed that most (>80%) of the T+ cells at this stage co-express Nanog (Figure 1H,I), confirming that T marks not only differentiating mesoderm but also pluripotent epiblast cells with a proximal posterior positional identity (Osorno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1H,I and citation to Osorno et al., 2012.

claim: The direct BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in a subpopulation of Nanog+ epiblast cells prior to overt mesoderm differentiation.
source: We conclude that the direct BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in a subpopulation of Nanog+ epiblast cells prior to overt mesoderm differentiation, in addition to its previously described expression in migrating mesoderm (Jen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented and cites Jen et al., 1997 for the previously described expression pattern.

claim: Id1 is expressed in migrating mesoderm.
source: We conclude that the direct BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in a subpopulation of Nanog+ epiblast cells prior to overt mesoderm differentiation, in addition to its previously described expression in migrating mesoderm (Jen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jen et al., 1997.

claim: BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1.
source: We used Sox1-GFP reporter ES cells (Ying et al., 2003b) to confirm that BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1 (Figure 2B) and permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T (Figure 2C,D), as expected (Ying et al., 2003a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and citations to Ying et al., 2003a and 2003b.

claim: BMP4 permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T.
source: We used Sox1-GFP reporter ES cells (Ying et al., 2003b) to confirm that BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1 (Figure 2B) and permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T (Figure 2C,D), as expected (Ying et al., 2003a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D and citation to Ying et al., 2003a.

claim: BMP-treated cells do not progress to overt mesoderm differentiation despite expressing T.
source: However, despite expressing T, BMP-treated cells do not progress to overt mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differentiation of epiblast to mesoderm is characterised by the loss of Oct4 and Cdh1.
source: Differentiation of epiblast to mesoderm is characterised by the loss of Oct4 and Cdh1, whereas BMP4-treated cells remain uniformly Cdh1+ at least for the first 5 days of BMP treatment (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: BMP4-treated cells remain uniformly Cdh1+ at least for the first 5 days of BMP treatment.
source: Differentiation of epiblast to mesoderm is characterised by the loss of Oct4 and Cdh1, whereas BMP4-treated cells remain uniformly Cdh1+ at least for the first 5 days of BMP treatment (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In the presence of BMP4, downregulation of Oct4 is delayed.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of BMP4, downregulation of Oct4 is delayed, and markers that characterise EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation are not upregulated within the 5-day time frame of this experiment (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Markers that characterise EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation are not upregulated within 5 days in the presence of BMP4.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of BMP4, downregulation of Oct4 is delayed, and markers that characterise EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation are not upregulated within the 5-day time frame of this experiment (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: T is first expressed in the posterior proximal epiblast prior to overt mesoderm differentiation.
source: T is first expressed in the posterior proximal epiblast prior to overt mesoderm differentiation (Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005) (see also Figure 1H,I) and marks a mesoderm-primed pluripotent state (Kubo et al., 2004; Bernemann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005 and data in Figure 1H,I.

claim: T marks a mesoderm-primed pluripotent state.
source: T is first expressed in the posterior proximal epiblast prior to overt mesoderm differentiation (Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005) (see also Figure 1H,I) and marks a mesoderm-primed pluripotent state (Kubo et al., 2004; Bernemann et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kubo et al., 2004 and Bernemann et al., 2011.

claim: In the presence of BMP4, T is coexpressed with Cdh1.
source: In support of this idea, we found that in the presence of BMP4, T is coexpressed with Cdh1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A subpopulation of cells (typically between 10 and 25%) differentiate into a Cdh1+ Tcfap2a (AP2α)+ epithelial cell type similar to early surface ectoderm in the presence of BMP4.
source: Not all cells persist in a T+ Cdh1+ state: a subpopulation of cells (typically between 10 and 25%) are able to differentiate into a Cdh1+ Tcfap2a (AP2α)+ epithelial cell type similar to early surface ectoderm (Mitchell et al., 1991) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Mitchell et al., 1991.

claim: Exogenous BMP4 promotes surface ectoderm differentiation when added to explants from the E7.0 mouse epiblast.
source: This is consistent with the recent finding that exogenous BMP4 promotes surface ectoderm differentiation when added to explants from the E7.0 mouse epiblast (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: BMP4, in the absence of other exogenous signals, imposes a T+ mesoderm-primed posterior positional identity but prevents cells from downregulating Cdh1.
source: We conclude that BMP4, in the absence of other exogenous signals, imposes a T+ mesoderm-primed posterior positional identity but prevents cells from downregulating Cdh1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BMP-treated cells are delayed in their differentiation and either persist in a Cdh1+ posterior-epiblast like state or ultimately differentiate into Cdh1+ surface-ectoderm-like cells.
source: BMP-treated cells are delayed in their differentiation and either persist in a Cdh1+ posterior-epiblast like state or ultimately differentiate into Cdh1+ surface-ectoderm-like cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data and illustrated in Figure 2E.

claim: Dox-mediated induction of Id1 is able to block neural induction.
source: We first confirmed that dox-mediated induction of Id1 is able to block neural induction as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Id1 delays the loss of Cdh1 under serum-free monolayer conditions in the absence of exogenous growth factors.
source: Under serum-free monolayer conditions in the absence of exogenous growth factors, Id1 delays the loss of Cdh1 and suppresses the upregulation of EMT markers Cdh2, Zeb1 and Zeb2 (Thiery et al., 2009) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Id1 suppresses the upregulation of EMT markers Cdh2, Zeb1 and Zeb2.
source: Under serum-free monolayer conditions in the absence of exogenous growth factors, Id1 delays the loss of Cdh1 and suppresses the upregulation of EMT markers Cdh2, Zeb1 and Zeb2 (Thiery et al., 2009) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Thiery et al., 2009.

claim: Id1 promotes the upregulation of T, a marker of posterior epiblast and primitive streak.
source: Id1 promotes the upregulation of T, a marker of posterior epiblast and primitive streak (Blum et al., 1992; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005), but delays the downregulation of the epiblast markers Oct4, Fgf5 and Otx2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Blum et al., 1992 and Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005.

claim: Id1 delays the downregulation of the epiblast markers Oct4, Fgf5 and Otx2.
source: Id1 promotes the upregulation of T, a marker of posterior epiblast and primitive streak (Blum et al., 1992; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005), but delays the downregulation of the epiblast markers Oct4, Fgf5 and Otx2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog, which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast.
source: In keeping with this idea, Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog, which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast, and Id1 also reduces expression of Sox2, which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast (Osorno et al., 2012) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Osorno et al., 2012.

claim: Id1 reduces expression of Sox2, which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast.
source: In keeping with this idea, Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog, which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast, and Id1 also reduces expression of Sox2, which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast (Osorno et al., 2012) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Osorno et al., 2012.

claim: Nanog marks posterior pluripotent epiblast.
source: In keeping with this idea, Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog, which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast, and Id1 also reduces expression of Sox2, which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast (Osorno et al., 2012) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Osorno et al., 2012.

claim: Sox2 marks anterior pluripotent epiblast.
source: In keeping with this idea, Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog, which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast, and Id1 also reduces expression of Sox2, which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast (Osorno et al., 2012) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Osorno et al., 2012.

claim: Markers of naïve pluripotency (Klf4, Rex1 and Esrrb) are rapidly lost in Id1 overexpressing cells.
source: We confirmed that Nanog in this context is likely to be marking a posterior epiblast-like cell rather than an earlier naïve pluripotent state because other markers of naïve pluripotency, Klf4, Rex1 and Esrrb, are rapidly lost in Id1 overexpressing cells, as they are in control cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: In the presence of exogenous Id1, T+ cells remain predominantly Cdh1+ and >90% of them coexpress Oct4.
source: In further support of the idea that Id1 delays differentiation, we used quantitative immunofluorescence to demonstrate that in the presence of exogenous Id1, T+ cells remain predominantly Cdh1+ and >90% of them coexpress Oct4 (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: T+ cells that coexpress Cdh1 and Oct4 are unlikely to be differentiated mesoderm cells and are more likely to be equivalent to the T+ cells in the proximal epiblast of the early embryo that have not yet entered the primitive streak.
source: These T+ cells are therefore unlikely to be differentiated mesoderm cells and are more likely to be equivalent to the T+ cells in the proximal epiblast of the early embryo that have not yet entered the primitive streak (Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data supported by citation to Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005.

claim: Dox treatment does not entirely block differentiation in dox-inducible Id1 cells.
source: Dox treatment does not entirely block differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurons begin to emerge in dox-treated cultures after 5 days.
source: Neurons begin to emerge in the dox-treated cultures after 5 days.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: Neurons that emerge in dox-treated cultures do not express the Flag-tagged Id1 transgenic protein.
source: However, these neurons do not express the Flag-tagged Id1 transgenic protein.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: Around 50% of cells are negative for Flag on day 5 in dox-treated cultures.
source: Indeed, around 50% of cells are negative for Flag on day 5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Constitutive Id1 expression is sufficient to completely block neurogenesis throughout the culture.
source: Unlike the dox-inducible system, this constitutive expression system is sufficient to completely block neurogenesis throughout the culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Constitutive Id1 expression is sufficient to delay the downregulation of Oct4.
source: Constitutive Id1 expression is sufficient to delay the downregulation of Oct4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and to block neurogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Constitutive Id1 expression is not sufficient to completely block differentiation.
source: However, it is not sufficient to completely block differentiation.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: Id1-overexpressing cells eventually differentiate predominantly into mesoderm rather than neurectoderm or endoderm, even under neural differentiation conditions.
source: Id1-overexpressing cells eventually differentiate predominantly into mesoderm rather than neurectoderm or endoderm, even under neural differentiation conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The BMP target gene Id1 does not drive overt mesoderm differentiation but rather maintains Cdh1 and helps to maintain a primed pluripotent state similar to that of the post-implantation epiblast, whilst imposing a proximal posterior (T+ Nanog+) epiblast identity that is primed for mesoderm differentiation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the BMP target gene Id1 does not drive overt mesoderm differentiation but rather maintains Cdh1 and helps to maintain a primed pluripotent state similar to that of the post-implantation epiblast, whilst imposing a proximal posterior (T+ Nanog+) epiblast identity that is primed for mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cdh1 is downregulated during the early stages of neural tube formation in vivo.
source: We wondered how this may relate to the ability of BMP to block neural induction, given that Cdh1 is downregulated during the early stages of neural tube formation in vivo (Hatta and Takeichi, 1986; Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996; Karpowicz et al., 2007) and during neural differentiation of ES cells (Sterneckert et al., 2010; Kamiya et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hatta and Takeichi, 1986; Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996; and Karpowicz et al., 2007.

claim: Cdh1 is downregulated during neural differentiation of ES cells.
source: We wondered how this may relate to the ability of BMP to block neural induction, given that Cdh1 is downregulated during the early stages of neural tube formation in vivo (Hatta and Takeichi, 1986; Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996; Karpowicz et al., 2007) and during neural differentiation of ES cells (Sterneckert et al., 2010; Kamiya et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sterneckert et al., 2010 and Kamiya et al., 2011.

claim: Cdh1 is largely absent from cells that have upregulated early neural markers.
source: We confirmed that Cdh1 is largely absent from cells that have upregulated early neural markers (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a close correlation between the expression of Cdh1 and Oct4 at all stages of the differentiation process.
source: Strikingly, we also observed a close correlation between the expression of Cdh1 and Oct4 at all stages of the differentiation process (Figure 4B), consistent with the idea that Cdh1 is downregulated at precisely the time that cells transit from Oct4+ epiblast towards neurectodermal differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cdh1 is downregulated at precisely the time that cells transit from Oct4+ epiblast towards neurectodermal differentiation.
source: Strikingly, we also observed a close correlation between the expression of Cdh1 and Oct4 at all stages of the differentiation process (Figure 4B), consistent with the idea that Cdh1 is downregulated at precisely the time that cells transit from Oct4+ epiblast towards neurectodermal differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cdh1 and Oct4 protein expression decline in synchrony within the developing neuroepithelium.
source: We confirmed a similar correlation between loss of Oct4 and downregulation of Cdh1 in vivo: Cdh1 and Oct4 protein expression decline in synchrony within the developing neuroepithelium (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Around 20–40% of cells fail to become Sox1-GFP+ after 4 days under uniform monolayer differentiation conditions.
source: Under these conditions, around 20–40% of cells fail to become Sox1-GFP+ after 4 days; around half of these persist as undifferentiated ES cells whilst the other half differentiate into non-neural (Sox1-negative) cell types (Ying and Smith, 2003; Lowell et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments and citations to Ying and Smith, 2003 and Lowell et al., 2006.

claim: Around half of the cells that fail to become Sox1-GFP+ persist as undifferentiated ES cells whilst the other half differentiate into non-neural (Sox1-negative) cell types.
source: Under these conditions, around 20–40% of cells fail to become Sox1-GFP+ after 4 days; around half of these persist as undifferentiated ES cells whilst the other half differentiate into non-neural (Sox1-negative) cell types (Ying and Smith, 2003; Lowell et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments and citations to Ying and Smith, 2003 and Lowell et al., 2006.

claim: The subpopulation of cells that fail to respond appropriately to a neural environment by upregulating Sox1-GFP also fail to downregulate Cdh1.
source: We observed that the subpopulation of cells that fail to respond appropriately to a neural environment by upregulating Sox1-GFP also fail to downregulate Cdh1, either remaining as Oct4+ Cdh1+ undifferentiated cells or differentiating into Cdh1+ Krt8+ epithelial cells (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Cells that fail to downregulate Cdh1 either remain as Oct4+ Cdh1+ undifferentiated cells or differentiate into Cdh1+ Krt8+ epithelial cells.
source: We observed that the subpopulation of cells that fail to respond appropriately to a neural environment by upregulating Sox1-GFP also fail to downregulate Cdh1, either remaining as Oct4+ Cdh1+ undifferentiated cells or differentiating into Cdh1+ Krt8+ epithelial cells (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Cdh1 is downregulated in synchrony with Oct4 during neural differentiation.
source: We conclude that Cdh1 is downregulated in synchrony with Oct4 during neural differentiation, and that heterogeneity in neural differentiation capacity within populations of ES cells is associated with a failure to downregulate Cdh1 in a subpopulation of those cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Heterogeneity in neural differentiation capacity within populations of ES cells is associated with a failure to downregulate Cdh1 in a subpopulation of those cells.
source: We conclude that Cdh1 is downregulated in synchrony with Oct4 during neural differentiation, and that heterogeneity in neural differentiation capacity within populations of ES cells is associated with a failure to downregulate Cdh1 in a subpopulation of those cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suppression of Cdh1 via function blocking antibodies rescues neural differentiation in cells that fail to downregulate Cdh1.
source: We used function blocking antibodies (Yoshida-Noro et al., 1984) in order to abolish the adhesive abilities of Cdh1. Blocking antibodies were added to Sox1-GFP reporter cells for the first 48 hr of neural differentiation and then removed, whereupon the cells rapidly regain normal cell-cell contacts. 1 day later, a minority of control cells are just starting to express Sox1-GFP, whereas the antibody-treated cells show strong Sox1-GFP expression throughout the culture. By the fourth day of differentiation, the antibody-treated cultures are almost uniformly Sox1-GFP+ (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B and citation to Yoshida-Noro et al., 1984.

claim: Early transient exposure to Cdh1 blocking antibody accelerates the loss of the pluripotency marker Oct4 and the gain of the neural marker Sox1.
source: qRT-PCR analysis confirmed that early transient exposure to the blocking antibody accelerates the loss of the pluripotency marker Oct4 and the gain of the neural marker Sox1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Transient loss of Cdh1 activity at the very start of the differentiation process is sufficient to drive ES cells efficiently towards neural differentiation.
source: This indicates that transient loss of Cdh1 activity at the very start of the differentiation process is sufficient to drive ES cells efficiently towards neural differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cdh1 null ES cells differentiate into neural cells more rapidly and efficiently in comparison with parental controls.
source: As an alternative loss-of-function approach, we made use of Cdh1 null ES cells (Larue et al., 1996). These cells do not form adherens junctions but do self-renew and retain multilineage differentiation potency. Cdh1 null ES cells differentiate into neural cells more rapidly and efficiently in comparison with parental controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and citation to Larue et al., 1996.

claim: Cdh1 null ES cells do not form adherens junctions but do self-renew and retain multilineage differentiation potency.
source: As an alternative loss-of-function approach, we made use of Cdh1 null ES cells (Larue et al., 1996). These cells do not form adherens junctions but do self-renew and retain multilineage differentiation potency.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments and citation to Larue et al., 1996.

claim: The transcription factor Twist1 is able to downregulate Cdh1 when bound to its heterodimerisation partner E47.
source: The transcription factor Twist1 is able to downregulate Cdh1 when bound to its heterodimerisation partner E47 (Thiery et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thiery et al., 2009.

claim: TwistE efficiently downregulates Cdh1 when expressed in ES cells by episomal transfection.
source: We confirmed that TwistE efficiently downregulates Cdh1 when expressed in ES cells by episomal transfection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Activation of TwistE has a striking ability to accelerate neural differentiation.
source: We reasoned that if downregulation of Cdh1 is a limiting requirement for neural induction, activation of TwistE should be able to enhance the efficiency of this process. This is indeed the case: activation of TwistE has a striking ability to accelerate neural differentiation.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: Cells treated with dox to activate TwistE generate extensive networks of neurons after only 3 days of exposure to neural conditions, whilst untreated control sister dishes do not start to generate significant numbers of neurons until day 5.
source: Cells that are treated with dox generate extensive networks of neurons after only 3 days of exposure to neural conditions, whilst untreated control sister dishes do not start to generate significant numbers of neurons until day 5 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Neural markers Sox1, Zfp521, Zeb2, Blbp, Sox9, Mash1 and Math1 are upregulated prematurely and Oct4 is lost more quickly in dox-treated cultures that activate TwistE.
source: Neural markers Sox1, Zfp521, Zeb2, Blbp, Sox9, Mash1 and Math1are upregulated prematurely and Oct4 is lost more quickly in dox-treated cultures (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Activating TwistE only for the first day of differentiation is sufficient to accelerate the early neural programme.
source: Activating TwistE only for the first day of differentiation is sufficient to accelerate the early neural programme (Figure 5H), indicating that Cdh1 activity is normally a limiting factor at an early stage in the differentiation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cdh1 activity is normally a limiting factor at an early stage in the differentiation process.
source: Activating TwistE only for the first day of differentiation is sufficient to accelerate the early neural programme (Figure 5H), indicating that Cdh1 activity is normally a limiting factor at an early stage in the differentiation process.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Downregulation of Cdh1 is a limiting requirement for pluripotent cells to differentiate into neural cells.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that downregulation of Cdh1 is a limiting requirement for pluripotent cells to differentiate into neural cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 1 ng/ml of BMP4 is sufficient to almost entirely inhibit neural induction and to maintain Cdh1 expression.
source: 1 ng/ml of BMP4 is sufficient to almost entirely inhibit neural induction and to maintain Cdh1 expression (Figure 6A), as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Suppression of Cdh1 via dox-induction of TwistE is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation in the presence of 1 ng/ml BMP.
source: Strikingly, suppression of Cdh1 via dox-induction of TwistE is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation in the presence of 1 ng/ml BMP. Tuj1+ neurons can be readily found in dox-treated cultures but are only rarely found in control sister dishes (Figure 6A), and dox treatment rescues the expression of early neural markers Mash1, Zfp521, Sox9 and Pax3 to levels similar to those observed in the absence of exogenous BMP (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Dox treatment rescues the expression of early neural markers Mash1, Zfp521, Sox9 and Pax3 to levels similar to those observed in the absence of exogenous BMP in the presence of 1 ng/ml BMP4.
source: Strikingly, suppression of Cdh1 via dox-induction of TwistE is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation in the presence of 1 ng/ml BMP. Tuj1+ neurons can be readily found in dox-treated cultures but are only rarely found in control sister dishes (Figure 6A), and dox treatment rescues the expression of early neural markers Mash1, Zfp521, Sox9 and Pax3 to levels similar to those observed in the absence of exogenous BMP (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TwistE abolishes the ability of BMP4 to sustain the expression of epiblast markers Oct4, Cdh1, Fgf5 and T.
source: TwistE also abolishes the ability of BMP4 to sustain the expression of epiblast markers Oct4, Cdh1, Fgf5 and T (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Under conditions with 1 ng/ml BMP4, BMP acts primarily through Cdh1 to maintain the expression of epiblast markers and block the expression of neural markers.
source: We conclude that under these conditions BMP acts primarily through Cdh1 to maintain the expression of epiblast markers and block the expression of neural markers.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 5 ng/ml BMP4, activation of TwistE eliminates Cdh1 expression from the majority of cells and upregulates the mesenchymal and neural marker Vimentin.
source: Under these conditions, activation of TwistE eliminates Cdh1 expression from the majority of cells and upregulates the mesenchymal and neural marker Vimentin (Figure 6C), but we did not observe any Tuj1+ neurons either in the presence or the absence of dox treatment (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At 5 ng/ml BMP4, no Tuj1+ neurons are observed either in the presence or the absence of dox treatment to activate TwistE.
source: Under these conditions, activation of TwistE eliminates Cdh1 expression from the majority of cells and upregulates the mesenchymal and neural marker Vimentin (Figure 6C), but we did not observe any Tuj1+ neurons either in the presence or the absence of dox treatment (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experiments.

claim: 5 ng/ml BMP4 upregulates posterior epiblast markers whilst delaying overt differentiation into mesoderm and endoderm.
source: We next confirmed that 5 ng/ml BMP4 upregulates posterior epiblast markers whilst delaying overt differentiation into mesoderm and endoderm (Figure 6D, black bars), as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: At 5 ng/ml BMP4, suppression of Cdh1 via dox-induction of TwE efficiently rescues mesoderm and endoderm differentiation, but not neural differentiation.
source: Under these conditions, suppression of Cdh1 via dox-induction of TwE efficiently rescues mesoderm and endoderm differentiation, but not neural differentiation (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Part of the mechanism by which BMP helps to maintain pluripotency is through maintenance of Cdh1, which interferes with efficient neural and mesodermal differentiation.
source: We conclude that part of the mechanism by which BMP helps to maintain pluripotency is through maintenance of Cdh1, which interferes with efficient neural and mesodermal differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Higher levels of BMP impose a posterior identity that primes cells for mesoderm and is incompatible with a neural fate.
source: Higher levels of BMP also impose a posterior identity that primes cells for mesoderm and is incompatible with a neural fate.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BMP can at the same time protect pluripotency and promote mesoderm differentiation.
source: Taken together, these findings help to explain why BMP can at the same time protect pluripotency and promote mesoderm differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Downregulation of Cdh1 is associated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) that accompanies the formation of mesoderm at the primitive streak.
source: For example, downregulation of Cdh1 is associated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) that accompanies the formation of mesoderm at the primitive streak and the emergence of neural crest cells from the dorsal neural tube (Thiery et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thiery et al., 2009.

claim: Downregulation of Cdh1 is associated with the emergence of neural crest cells from the dorsal neural tube.
source: For example, downregulation of Cdh1 is associated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) that accompanies the formation of mesoderm at the primitive streak and the emergence of neural crest cells from the dorsal neural tube (Thiery et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thiery et al., 2009.

claim: The formation of the early neural plate from the epiblast is accompanied by loss of Cdh1 and gain of N-Cadherin (Cdh2) and Vimentin.
source: The formation of the early neural plate from the epiblast does not bear all the hallmarks of a classical EMT, but it is accompanied by loss of Cdh1 and gain of N-Cadherin (Cdh2) and Vimentin (Hatta and Takeichi, 1986; Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hatta and Takeichi, 1986 and Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996.

claim: EMT is required for overt mesoderm differentiation.
source: There is already evidence that EMT is required for overt mesoderm differentiation (Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010), and we find here that downregulation of Cdh1 is similarly a limiting event for neural differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010.

claim: BMP signalling contributes to the maintenance of pluripotency.
source: Although it is well established that BMP signalling contributes to the maintenance of pluripotency (Ying et al., 2003a; Di-Gregorio et al., 2007), the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ying et al., 2003a and Di-Gregorio et al., 2007.

claim: BMP suppresses differentiation by maintaining expression of Cdh1.
source: We propose that BMP suppresses differentiation by maintaining expression of Cdh1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suppressing Cdh1 is sufficient to rescue the BMP-imposed block to multilineage differentiation.
source: We support this idea by showing that suppressing Cdh1 is sufficient to rescue the BMP-imposed block to multilineage differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BMP target gene Id1 imposes a proximal posterior identity on undifferentiated cells, priming them towards mesoderm.
source: We find that the BMP target gene Id1 imposes a proximal posterior identity on undifferentiated cells, priming them towards mesoderm.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ability of Id1 to block neural differentiation is unlikely to be explained entirely by inhibition of a neural-inducing transcription factor or by a direct activation of mesoderm differentiation, but rather to a shift in the positional identity of pluripotent cells that occurs in the absence of overt differentiation.
source: The ability of Id1 to block neural differentiation is therefore unlikely to be explained entirely by inhibition of a neural-inducing transcription factor as is commonly assumed, nor by a direct activation of mesoderm differentiation, but rather to a shift in the positional identity of pluripotent cells that occurs in the absence of overt differentiation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Id1 null ES cells have a defect in the maintenance of pluripotency.
source: Id1 null ES cells have a defect in the maintenance of pluripotency (Romero-Lanman et al., 2011), consistent with our finding that Id1 delays exit from an epiblast-like state.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romero-Lanman et al., 2011.

claim: Id1 has an earlier pre-implantation role to suppress the activity of Tcf15.
source: We note, though, that the Id1 null phenotype is also likely to reflect an earlier pre-implantation role for Id1: to suppress the activity of Tcf15 (Davies et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2013.

claim: Suppression of Tcf15 by Id1 maintains expression of Nanog and suppresses the transition to a T+ epiblast-like state.
source: The consequence of this would be to maintain expression of Nanog and suppress the transition to a T+ epiblast-like state (Davies et al., 2013), in keeping with the Id1 null ES cell phenotype (Romero-Lanman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2013 and Romero-Lanman et al., 2011.

claim: The two effects of BMP, to maintain Cdh1 and to impose a posterior identity, can be uncoupled by varying the dose of BMP.
source: The two effects of BMP, to maintain Cdh1 and to impose a posterior identity, can be uncoupled by varying the dose of BMP.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lower doses of BMP are sufficient to maintain Cdh1 and to suppress neural fate, but insufficient to impose a stable posterior identity.
source: Lower doses of BMP are sufficient to maintain Cdh1 and to suppress neural fate, but insufficient to impose a stable posterior identity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suppressing Cdh1 at lower doses of BMP is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation.
source: Strikingly, suppressing Cdh1 at these lower doses of BMP is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation, indicating that the primary mechanism by which BMP inhibits neural differentiation in this context is through its ability to control Cadherin activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The primary mechanism by which BMP inhibits neural differentiation at lower doses is through its ability to control Cadherin activity.
source: Strikingly, suppressing Cdh1 at these lower doses of BMP is sufficient to rescue neural differentiation, indicating that the primary mechanism by which BMP inhibits neural differentiation in this context is through its ability to control Cadherin activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cdh1 influences growth factor receptiveness of ES cells.
source: There is a growing body of evidence that Cdh1 influences growth factor receptiveness of ES cells, and that it can consequently stabilise particular pluripotent states (Chou et al., 2008; Soncin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Redmer et al., 2011; Hawkins et al., 2012; del Valle et al., 2013; Faunes et al., 2013), but it is not known what controls Cdh1 expression in this context.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cdh1 can stabilise particular pluripotent states.
source: There is a growing body of evidence that Cdh1 influences growth factor receptiveness of ES cells, and that it can consequently stabilise particular pluripotent states (Chou et al., 2008; Soncin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Redmer et al., 2011; Hawkins et al., 2012; del Valle et al., 2013; Faunes et al., 2013), but it is not known what controls Cdh1 expression in this context.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: BMP/Id maintains Cdh1 expression during differentiation of ES cells.
source: We fill this gap with our finding that BMP/Id maintains Cdh1 expression during differentiation of ES cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Id1 is excluded from the anterior streak in vivo.
source: Interestingly, Id1 is excluded from the anterior streak in vivo (Jen et al., 1997), so it is possible that it plays a more general role in regulating EMT in the early embryo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jen et al., 1997.

claim: Id1 may play a more general role in regulating EMT in the early embryo.
source: Interestingly, Id1 is excluded from the anterior streak in vivo (Jen et al., 1997), so it is possible that it plays a more general role in regulating EMT in the early embryo.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observation that Id1 is excluded from the anterior streak.

claim: BMP signals generated from the extraembryonic ectoderm block neural induction in vivo.
source: In vivo, the BMP signals that are generated from the extraembryonic ectoderm not only block neural induction but are also required for formation of mesoderm (Mishina et al., 1995; Winnier et al., 1995; Lawson et al., 1999; Beppu et al., 2000; Davis et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: BMP signals generated from the extraembryonic ectoderm are required for formation of mesoderm in vivo.
source: In vivo, the BMP signals that are generated from the extraembryonic ectoderm not only block neural induction but are also required for formation of mesoderm (Mishina et al., 1995; Winnier et al., 1995; Lawson et al., 1999; Beppu et al., 2000; Davis et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: BMP signalling is necessary for maintenance of pluripotency.
source: However, BMP signalling is also necessary for maintenance of pluripotency (Di-Gregorio et al., 2007), and mouse embryos in which BMP has been experimentally overactivated have an impairment in mesoderm differentiation that cannot easily be explained by models in which BMP drives mesoderm differentiation (Aoyama et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Di-Gregorio et al., 2007.

claim: Mouse embryos in which BMP has been experimentally overactivated have an impairment in mesoderm differentiation.
source: However, BMP signalling is also necessary for maintenance of pluripotency (Di-Gregorio et al., 2007), and mouse embryos in which BMP has been experimentally overactivated have an impairment in mesoderm differentiation that cannot easily be explained by models in which BMP drives mesoderm differentiation (Aoyama et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aoyama et al., 2012.

claim: BMP can prime cells for mesoderm fate by imposing a posterior identity, but restrain them from undergoing overt mesoderm formation by suppressing EMT.
source: Our findings unite these observations by showing how BMP can prime cells for mesoderm fate by imposing a posterior identity, but restrain them from undergoing overt mesoderm formation by suppressing EMT.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In frogs, antagonism of BMP by the organiser induces anterior-posterior axis formation.
source: In frogs, antagonism of BMP by the organiser induces anterior-posterior axis formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: BMP antagonism acts by stimulating mediolateral intercalation of caudal progenitors, releasing them to participate in the formation of the axis.
source: It has been proposed (Constance Lane et al., 2004) that BMP antagonism acts by stimulating mediolateral intercalation of caudal progenitors, releasing them to participate in the formation of the axis, and that the normal role of BMP is to preserve a reservoir of progenitors throughout axis elongation.

claim: The normal role of BMP is to preserve a reservoir of progenitors throughout axis elongation.

claim: BMP acts by a similar mechanism during differentiation of pluripotent mouse cells as it does in frogs, preserving a population of undifferentiated cells by preventing the loss of Cdh1.
source: We propose that BMP acts by a similar mechanism during differentiation of pluripotent mouse cells, preserving a population of undifferentiated cells by preventing the loss of Cdh1.

claim: BMP's ability to antagonise Nodal signalling may be connected with BMP's ability to control EMT.
source: This may be connected with BMP's ability to antagonise Nodal signalling, given that Nodal is required for the initiation of EMT at the primitive streak (Arnold and Robertson, 2009; Yan et al., 2009).

claim: A subpopulation of ES cells tends to resist neural differentiation.

evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The subpopulation of cells that resist neural differentiation fail to respond appropriately to a neural-inducing environment because they are unable to downregulate Cdh1.

evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Experimental suppression of Cdh1 activity can rescue neural differentiation capacity in the recalcitrant subpopulation resulting in a more homogenous differentiation response.

evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Experimental suppression of Cdh1 can be achieved by non-genetic means, such as function-blocking E-Cadherin antibodies.
source: Importantly, this can be achieved by non-genetic means, such as function-blocking E-Cadherin antibodies, providing a convenient and readily applicable means to improve our control over pluripotent cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The loss of Cdh1 activity is a limiting event for the earliest stages of neural differentiation.
source: In summary, we have identified the loss of Cdh1 activity as a limiting event for the earliest stages of neural differentiation and we propose that BMP controls differentiation in part by maintaining Cdh1 expression.

claim: BMP controls differentiation in part by maintaining Cdh1 expression.

claim: The strategy of coupling changes in cell adhesion to transcriptional control of cell fate specification is used several times during development as a way of coordinating tissue morphogenesis.
source: The strategy of coupling changes in cell adhesion to transcriptional control of cell fate specification is used several times during development as a way of coordinating tissue morphogenesis (Owens et al., 2000; Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010; Watt and Fujiwara, 2011), and it will be interesting to investigate the implications of our findings for germ-layer formation in the early embryo.

claim: BMP signalling protects pluripotency and suppresses neural specification.

claim: BMP signalling is required for the formation of mesoderm in vivo.
